presentingComplaint: Progressive breathlessness and light-headedness over one week
history: 58-year-old man with a 7-day history of worsening exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea and vague retrosternal chest discomfort, now breathless at rest. Reports two episodes of near-syncope on standing. Background of metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer diagnosed 4 months ago on carboplatin/pemetrexed. No fever, no recent chest trauma or cardiac intervention. Non-anticoagulated.
examination: Anxious, cool peripheries. Markedly raised JVP with a prominent x-descent, quiet/muffled heart sounds and no pericardial rub. Palpable pulsus paradoxus. Chest clear to auscultation with no basal crackles and no focal consolidation. No calf swelling or tenderness; no focal neurological deficit.
imaging: CXR: enlarged, globular 'water-bottle' cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Transthoracic echo: large circumferential pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium and right ventricle, dilated non-collapsing IVC, and >25% respirophasic variation in mitral inflow (echo tamponade physiology).
differentialDiagnoses: Acute decompensated heart failure / pulmonary oedema
finalDiagnosis: Cardiac tamponade due to malignant pericardial effusion
citations: ESC Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases 2015
contraindications: Avoid aggressive diuresis and vasodilators (nitrates, ACE inhibitors) - preload-dependent state; may precipitate haemodynamic collapse
Positive-pressure ventilation can worsen venous return and cause arrest - secure haemodynamics/pericardiocentesis first
edgeCases: Low-pressure tamponade in hypovolaemic patients may lack overt hypotension and pulsus paradoxus
Pulsus paradoxus can be absent with coexisting aortic regurgitation, severe LV dysfunction, or large ASD; loculated effusions (e.g. post-surgical) can cause regional tamponade
expectedMaiK: Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) with pulsus paradoxus and an enlarged cardiac silhouette in a patient with malignancy points to cardiac tamponade - a non-infective obstructive shock. Urgent bedside echo confirms right-heart diastolic collapse, and emergency echo-guided pericardiocentesis is both diagnostic and life-saving; avoid diuretics/vasodilators and delay of positive-pressure ventilation.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg, and any history of malignancy, recent cardiac procedure, uraemia or TB exposure?
Any preceding chest trauma, aortic dissection features, or anticoagulant use?
expectedInvestigations: Pericardial fluid analysis and cytology after drainage
regressionAssertions: differential must include heart_failure and pe
